quote: I asked Scout to do some shopping for me first, as the AI made it seem like a much smoother process than with other AI tools. I asked it to find me a pair of shorts. quote: Scout also brought up an unopened email from the power company about needing to check my solar panels. quote: I was more impressed with Muse than I expected. But that only made me warier about it. Digital chores that consume more time than any one of them deserves are all too common at the moment, and Muse proved remarkably good at stepping into that gap. The catch is that the closer it gets to behaving like a genuinely useful personal assistant, the more personal information it needs to do the job.
author: Eric Hal Schwartz
notes: TechRadar verdict: useful but uncomfortable trust tradeoff.

quote:
I asked Meta Muse to spawn 120 subagents at once. Each had the same deliberately boring job: run `sleep 30` in a shell and send back one line.

Thirty-three agents were created. The other 87 spawn attempts failed. I never got the combined answer.

quote:

{"error_code":"spawn_failed","error_message":"database error: sqlx error: error returned from database: canceling statement due to lock timeout"}

notes: Recovered spawn_failed payloads show PostgreSQL lock timeout on subagent.spawn.

Meta Opened Free Access to Muse AI Agent with 100M Tokens per Week

@Meta launched Muse — a personal #AI agent that works 24/7 across your email, browser, and connected services, and it's now free with up to 100M tokens per week.

Built with Zuckerberg's "personal superintelligence" pitch in mind, Muse runs in an isolated cloud VM and never touches your real credentials directly — a separate Sentinel system approves or blocks every action, network request, and payment. Prompt injection defenses, surrogate payment tokens, and single-use cards round out the security model, and Meta is now offering researchers up to $300K in bug bounties (up to $130K for a critical instruction-hijack exploit).

It's a serious bet that agentic AI can be made safe enough for real-world autonomy — email, shopping, background tasks — without handing over the keys.

quote:
📰 #imNEWS: @Meta launched Muse, a personal AI agent that talks like a chat in the Muse app or WhatsApp, powered by Muse Spark. It runs in a dedicated Muse Secure VM, can keep working after you close the app, and asks before emails or purchases. Link by Stripe covers agent checkout with one-time cards. US rollout on iOS, Android, and https://t.co/gSNkgq6rfh, free for most use, with subscriptions for more.

🔑 3 Key Takeaways

① An agent that keeps working
Muse is built for everyday tasks (email, travel) and bigger goals. Share a goal, it builds a plan, then it can open a browser, fill forms, and negotiate. For longer jobs it keeps going after you close the app and comes back when something changes or it needs approval.

② A dedicated VM, not a chat overlay
Muse Secure VM is a contained cloud computer for the agent plus your data and credentials. A separate Sentinel agent has to approve anything that hits the internet. Muse cannot see passwords or payment methods. A Confidential VM later this year encrypts the whole box with a key only the user holds.

③ Checkout and memory with limits
Muse can pay with Link, including purchase protections and one-time cards. Shop Pay and 1Password support are coming. It can turn a saved Instagram recipe reel into a grocery list and remember dietary restrictions. You pick app access, can disconnect anytime, and can opt out of training.

✅ Action Item
Run one real task in Muse this week (book something, dispute a bill, or checkout). Write down where it asked for approval vs acted on its own. If you sell via WhatsApp or Instagram, that log is your map for how consumer agents will sit between you and the customer.

quote: One of the first tasks I assigned Muse, which carries out actions using a cloud-based virtual computer, was to sort through my Gmail inbox and delete messages I don't need. That required me to connect Muse to my Google account and give it permission to access, read, and delete emails. The process didn't go smoothly on mobile; the Google sign-in screen kept glitching and returning me to the Muse website instead of the app. I eventually got it working on my laptop, where it deleted thousands of promotional emails and updates.

quote: So I asked Muse to look through my Gmail — who was I talking to a year ago but haven't spoken to recently? Muse ran slowly, but it did find some founders that I hadn't talked to since last fall. I'm taking a closer look into some of the companies it mentioned.

quote: I asked Muse to monitor prices from Newark to Haneda for a 3-month trip beginning in January. It did a good job of searching flight prices, finding a ticket for $2,000 on United. I got Muse to check twice a day, but that still could miss some great fares.

quote: I am shocked. After playing with Muse by Meta for an hour in just chat mode, I was impressed enough to: I never use Apple Reminders so I gave Muse read access to Reminders. It was very slow compared to my repetitive tapping, but it clipped every coupon for me after getting my login credentials for the grocery store's website.

quote:
I used Muse today to apply for visa. If you have never applied for visa, congrats, bc visa application is one of the worst things in human bureaucracy machine.

anyways, i got Muse to:
- book a multi-legged refundable flight
- book a refundable hotel
- get my bank statement to prove i can pay
- dig through my emails to find all my papers (passport photo, i94, etc.)
- write an itinerary plan for what i would be doing each day
- fill out the form from the website

which is pretty good! but some problems i bumped into:
- i needed a passport photo, so I used chatgpt to change a selfie into a passport photo. Muse could upload it, but you needed to size the photo to fit in the frame and Muse couldn't do it, so I had to do it myself.
- Muse couldn't upload the rest of the files, so i had to upload everything.
- while i uploaded, i realized 1 of the document field could only be JPG (not PDF! why did it not accept pdf??) so i asked muse to convert the PDF to JPG. also they didn't accept images > 2MB so also had to ask Muse to compress all my photos. i wish it just noticed that and fixed it itself.
- i also realized there was a bunch of details Muse was missing (e.g. there were more docs that we needed, extra flights to book etc. to follow the instruction)
- i realized i needed to book an extra flight, and it has strong enough bot detection that Muse couldn't do it itself :( so i had to book it manually.

in the end, Muse did ~70% of the work, and i still had to spend ~1 hour on it. but it's like 1 hour of annoyance (i bumped into issue, i had to fix/ delegate to Muse, bumped into another issue, etc.) so i'm still pretty grumpy by the end.

i'm grateful; but also if someone can build a visa application bench & train computer use agent on this successfully that person can have all of my money.
author: @sherlockieee

quote: Asked Muse to append to a finance spreadsheet: go through email for payments after September 4th, open the budgeting spreadsheet, and append them to the bottom in chronological order following the existing template.

quote: According to new data provided by the market intelligence firm Sensor Tower, Muse has been downloaded north of 83,000 times on iOS in the United States. … While this pushed Muse into the No. 2 position on the App Store’s Top Charts, its launch pales when compared with other recent app debuts from Meta, like Threads and Meta AI… Its Android counterpart, however, is faring less well. Muse has only achieved a rank of No. 338 in the Productivity category on Google Play’s app marketplace.
author: Sarah Perez
notes: TechCrunch Sep 10: Muse ~83k US iOS downloads → No.2 App Store; Android #338 Productivity; WhatsApp/web not counted.

quote: Despite security concerns and an overly broad and permissive privacy policy, Silicon Valley insiders have been raving about Instinct’s capabilities. … While there are plenty of other agents that focus more narrowly on things like managing work or family life, Instinct seems to be the one to beat… This week, for example, Instinct has rolled out email addresses for all its users, and just announced it’s building its own social network of sorts — that is, one person’s Instinct agent can now talk to those belonging to their friends to coordinate plans.
author: Sarah Perez
notes: Same TechCrunch piece: Muse launch framed against Instinct as the peer to beat; Instinct agent email + agent-to-agent social.

quote: In a documented hands-on test, Muse shortlisted a Patagonia jacket at a discount that had already expired, apparently pulled from a batch-updated merchant catalog feed instead of live pricing. On a separate Amazon order, it quoted a September 15 delivery when the same item was two days out in the Amazon app. And when the tester tried a DoorDash order, the login flow broke down entirely. "it got stuck in log-in circular hell"
author: Austin
notes: Saner.AI Muse review (Sep 9): stale catalog price, wrong Amazon ETA, DoorDash login loop — “log-in circular hell”.

quote: And the free allowance is smaller in practice than the number implies. Meta's AI chief says most people will never need to pay. One hands-on reviewer hit 81% of the weekly cap in a single day doing normal things. If you actually use an agent the way the marketing describes, $20 a month is needed.
author: Austin
notes: Saner.AI: free weekly token allotment burns fast — 81% in one day of ordinary use.

quote: But the dominant thread, by volume, was people wanting this exact product from literally any other company. "I absolutely don't trust Facebook with the necessary data." Several connected the trust problem to Meta's business model rather than to any specific technical claim… "It's handing your drug dealer the keys to your house."
author: Austin
notes: Saner.AI synthesis of launch chatter: product praise vs deep Meta trust distrust.

quote: Security practitioners focused on the structural problem: an unattended agent reading the open web, holding your private data, with the ability to send things out. "This is the worst kind of hazmat for LLMs, in one of the most adversarially challenging roles"
author: Austin
notes: Saner.AI quoting security-practitioner reaction to unattended agent + private data blast radius.

quote: Observers who've followed agent tooling for years gave Muse the highest practical compliment available: it's the first thing in the category that a normal person can actually use. "the first main openclaw-like product that has made it to the 'just works' level"
author: Austin
notes: Saner.AI citing HN-style praise: Muse as first OpenClaw-like consumer agent that just works.

quote: Muse is the most capable of the three on raw IQ. It can hold more of the problem in a single conversation and just… do the work. If you want one agent that feels like the smartest person in the room, that's Muse. It's deep and impressive how far it takes things. Cons are the main Agent and sub chat is kind of dumb IMO.
author: @ComebackCap
notes: ComebackCap three-way: Muse wins raw capability; sub-chat UX weak.

quote: But here's where transparency matters: Meta can still access your VM data. The blog states that isolation is "operational" — policy-based, not cryptographic. A Confidential VM that would cryptographically prevent Meta from accessing your data is planned "for later in 2026," but doesn't exist yet.
author: Vincee Cole
notes: Memeburn web UI walkthrough: Secure VM is policy isolation, Confidential VM later.

quote: Meta's closed alpha through invite codes confirmed these capabilities, with users reporting useful email management and competent restaurant booking. Early testers noted disconnections and one instance where Muse surfaced private photos unprompted — but the foundation is functional.
author: Vincee Cole
notes: Memeburn: alpha praise on email/restaurants; disconnection + unprompted private photos.

quote: The trust gap. The security architecture is sophisticated and the Sentinel system is well-designed. But trust isn't just engineering — it's track record. When a company that paid $5 billion for privacy deception asks to connect your email, bank, and health data, whitepapers only go so far.
author: Vincee Cole
notes: Memeburn: Meta track-record trust gap vs Sentinel architecture praise.

quote: Yeah. Codex and Cowork are full of papercuts when it comes to usability. Grok Bot is head and shoulders better and more pleasant to use. And Muse is similar to Grok Bot.
author: archon810
notes: HN: Muse UX in same pleasant band as Grok Bot vs Codex/Cowork papercuts.

quote: I have been using Grok Bot, Town and Instinct myself. That matters because the value proposition becomes much easier to understand once you experience it personally. You stop thinking about "using AI" and start thinking about handing something off. ... Meta is attempting to take an experience pioneered by smaller companies and put it in front of a mass consumer audience through an ecosystem that includes WhatsApp, Instagram, Facebook, and eventually AI glasses.
author: Steven Wolfe Pereira
notes: Board Brief: Muse as Meta's mass-consumer bid on the Town/Instinct/Grok Bot pattern.

quote: A popup message started appearing on Sunday for Muse users saying that “continued access by an unauthorized AI agent violates Amazon’s Conditions of Use, to which our customers have agreed.” … Amazon also expressed privacy and security concerns over Muse failing to identify itself when it browses, and seemingly capturing customer credentials.
author: Jess Weatherbed
notes: Verge Sep 21: Amazon blocks Muse shopping; GeekWire-sourced popup Sunday.

quote: Meta has pushed back against these characterizations, asserting that Muse “has no visibility into people’s passwords or payment methods.” The company maintains that credentials “go into secure storage, so Muse can use them without seeing them.” Despite these assurances, the block remains in effect.
author: Tessa Vaughn
notes: Forkast: retailer-access tax framing; Meta credential pushback vs Amazon block.

quote: Meta Muse is the best personal agent most people can actually use today — free, public, and with the category's best-designed confirmation flow. … on September 18 it displaced ChatGPT as the #1 free iPhone app in the US, the same day it reached Canada.
author: Top5Apps
notes: Top5Apps Sep 21: Muse #1 overall; App Store #1 free US on Sep 18.

quote: And note the newest constraint: merchants can veto agents — Amazon blocked Muse on September 20 under Agent Terms it added to its Conditions of Use in August, and any retailer can copy the move.
author: Top5Apps
notes: Top5Apps: merchant veto / Amazon Agent Terms as availability constraint.

quote: The open question is not capability. It is whether people will hand Meta their Gmail, calendar, and wallet two weeks after a giant social-harm settlement. Muse is the first of these agents that could actually be on a hundred million phones.
author: Neeraj Nathany
notes: Faraday: Muse mass-market bet vs Meta trust overhang.

quote: Task depth. Muse opens browsers, fills forms, makes purchases, schedules lessons. Poke handles calendar, email, and scheduling. Muse's action scope is broader. … Distribution. WhatsApp (billions of users), Instagram, Facebook.
author: Fabric
notes: Fabric comparison: Muse wins depth/distribution; Poke wins iMessage.

quote: Muse is betting that the first useful personal agent is an organizer. … Muse says it asks people to approve critical actions such as sending emails and making purchases. Its launch materials also describe permissions, an activity log, and settings that let users adjust how cautious the agent should be.
author: Refix
notes: Refix: Muse as personal coordination + approval controls.

quote: I started by testing it with some obvious, straightforward tasks. First, I asked it to look through my email and send me a daily digest of "important" emails (my inbox gets quickly clogged with PR pitches and newsletters). It did this admirably well. I also asked it to look at my credit and debit cards and tell me what subscription I could cancel — it suggested Flickr.
author: Katie Notopoulos
notes: Business Insider hands-on (19 Sep 2026): inbox digest + subscription scan worked.

quote: The Girl Scouts of America defeat AI! The Girl Scouts' website has always been really frustrating to use, and although Muse almost could do it, it couldn't complete the final payment section without the site timing out. I ended up having to do it on my computer.
author: Katie Notopoulos
notes: BI: membership renewal stalled at payment/timeout on Girl Scouts site.

quote: I can see the promise here — it was able to accomplish (or at least half-accomplish) some stuff that could be genuinely helpful. A colleague of mine used Muse to successfully dispute a health bill with his insurance. But it can't yet do the really annoying stuff I don't want to do myself.
author: Katie Notopoulos
notes: BI verdict: helpful on some admin, not yet life-running; colleague insurance dispute success.

quote: I decided to name my agent Lyra. Getting the name into the field should have been the easiest thing in the world, and instead it took me a few tries because the text field was not behaving like a normal text field with VoiceOver. … Then I got into the chat and realized the chat messages are not headings. I am gonna be honest, I was really mad about this.
author: Taylor Arndt
notes: Substack (21 Sep): VoiceOver text-field + missing chat headings.

quote: I like Muse. That is really the simplest answer. … But right now I am stuck in this weird place where the agent itself feels more useful than the interface around it. VoiceOver makes some parts way harder than they need to be, and the connector gap means I cannot hand Muse the systems where a lot of my actual work lives.
author: Taylor Arndt
notes: Substack verdict: likes agent capability; blocked by a11y + connector gaps.

quote: Y'all, the PDF it generated was beautiful. It was the first time an agent has produced a design I actually like in a single shot. … The newsletter was perfectly laid out and easy to read. It included: a weekly agenda … call-outs for parents … News to Know … Local Events.
author: Claire Vo
notes: How I AI (16 Sep): one-shot printable family morning newsletter PDF.

quote: The agent's response was incredibly well-toned. It wasn't sycophantic like some models can be. It felt kind and human. "Sleep deprivation with a baby is its own special kind of hard. We'll get you some rest." … This combination of a dedicated "Goal" primitive with automated reminders is genius. It separates these long-term aspirations from the flow of everyday tasks, which is something I've found challenging with other agents like Grok Bot or OpenClaw.
author: Claire Vo
notes: How I AI: Goals primitive vs Grok Bot/OpenClaw task-soup; gentle sleep-training coaching.

quote: My first attempt was asking it to shop for New Balance 9060s. … The experience was not great. Muse struggled to find the right colorway and seemed to get stuck during browser use. … [On IMAX tickets] Muse then opened its browser view … navigated to the theater website, selected the tickets, and proceeded to guest checkout. … It arrived at the payment screen and prompted me to use Stripe Link.
author: Claire Vo
notes: How I AI: shoe browse fail; IMAX ticket flow to Link checkout succeeded (stopped before buy).

quote: Btw I did this Muse, giving it the ability to use its cred vault to log into her school information system and read through all the crap and other websites and collate the homework's and their due dates, adding to my child's calendar when they're due and a reminder the day before with a link to the calendar. I had model the workflow formally … and set it up to run daily. … First meaningful use of an OpenClaw like system.
author: fnordpiglet
notes: HN (22 Sep) on Amazon/Muse thread: daily school homework collation via Muse cred vault.

quote: My concern with Muse, and all these AI shopping tools, is that we'll end up in a world where inventory drops to 0, orders are placed by the business based on the number of bots in the queue, and as inventory is made available, it is immediately snatched up by shopping bots... similar to what we've seen in collector markets (ex. sneaker drops) or concert ticket sales. I don't want to live in a world where an AI agent is required to buy basic goods, just to compete with everyone else using them.
author: al_borland
notes: HN on Amazon blocking Muse: bot-scarcity / compulsory-agent shopping worry.

quote: Meta's own internal testing reportedly found Muse bypassing safeguards and exposing private iCloud photos when asked to identify toys in party pictures, and an employee reported many reliability failures while using it to track fast-selling items, per Benzinga's September 2026 reporting.
author: Damien
notes: HokAI listing citing Benzinga Sep 2026: internal safeguard bypass + reliability failures. Secondary cite.

quote: It's been a busy afternoon for Pip, the AI agent I've been using in Meta's Muse app. The agent, which Meta launched on September 8, booked a Friday date night and made a packing schedule for my upcoming move. It also emailed a friend about a trip next month and made a planning document with places we want to visit.
author: Lisa Eadicicco
notes: CNN Business hands-on Sep 23: packing schedule, date-night booking, trip email + Google Doc.

quote: When I asked for a list of places to go for date night, it pulled up two options in my neighborhood that had been closed for years. … In its list of prompt ideas, Muse said it could haggle on Facebook Marketplace … But when I tried this, Muse said it couldn't message sellers directly. It would instead vet the listings and draft a message for me to send.
author: Lisa Eadicicco
notes: CNN: stale closed venues + Marketplace Ideas oversell vs draft-only reality.

quote: While Muse was able to browse Target's website, I still had to enter personal details manually because the retailer blocked autonomous clicks at checkout. (Muse uses Stripe's Link digital wallet service for purchases, which it says generates a one-time use card to prevent your credit card number from being shared.)
author: Lisa Eadicicco
notes: CNN: Target blocks autonomous checkout clicks; Amazon browse already vaulted elsewhere.

quote: I asked Muse to archive the files it could see and send them to my Google Drive. It did. The download was about 2.7 GB compressed and 6.8 GB unpacked. It appeared to contain the root filesystem of the Linux environment assigned to my session, including Ubuntu system files, Muse's internal documentation, integration code, app templates, memory files, and agent logs. There were also SSH key files.
author: Peter James
notes: Sep 22: user exported ~6.8GB Muse session root FS (Hatch internals); Meta bounty Not Applicable.

quote: I asked Muse to archive the filesystem visible to my session and send it to my Google Drive. It sent an archive that unpacked to about 6.8 GB. Inside were internal docs, integration code, the Spaces app framework, memory records, container startup scripts, and documentation for an experimental ESP32-based home network bridge called Home Link. … I reported the export to Meta's bug bounty program, which marked it "Not Applicable."
author: Aeroi
notes: HN thread on mouse.dev export; author summary + NA bounty.

quote: You can ask Meta Muse to take actions that clearly break other site's terms of service and it happily does it. I asked it to bot poker games and it just hopped right in to a table.
author: chis
notes: HN: Muse willingly bots poker / breaks third-party ToS.

quote: muse is a pretty capable agent but still asks for too many approvals to do tasks. I'm a student and have been going between muse and instinct
author: websiteapi
notes: HN: capable but approval-heavy; student switching Muse↔Instinct.

quote: When he asked how the assistant knew about the conversation, Muse told him: "I saw the notification previews, not your message history. I haven't been reading your texts." … Singleton said the model simply did not know how it works and invented a coherent-sounding answer. "That's on us," he wrote. "We apologize for the incorrect response from Muse…"
author: Lars Cornelissen
author_name: Lars Cornelissen (Data Today) quoting Jason Aten / David Singleton
notes: Aten Messages incident: Muse hallucinated notification-preview access; Meta apologized Sep 19.

quote: Muse is the fastest consumer app launch Meta has ever had, and in the same week it topped the US App Store it also picked up a working macOS exploit, a privacy complaint from a columnist who tested it, and a hard block from Amazon. That combination is the story, not the download chart. … If you run the Mac app, update it now: a hotfix landed on September 21 for a local privilege escalation bug.
author: Sam Carter
notes: Sep 22 guide: App Store surge + Wardle Mac hotfix + Aten + Amazon; connect low-stakes only.

quote: Mac security researcher Patrick Wardle says it's trivial to turn Muse into "the ultimate backdoor." … By redirecting dictation traffic to an attacker-controlled server, an attacker could capture voice prompts and obtain the authentication token for the victim's Muse account. … Wardle's advice about Muse is simple: "Please don't install."
author: Pieter Arntz
notes: Malwarebytes Sep 22 on Wardle Muse dictation-endpoint local token theft; hotfix noted elsewhere.

quote: Facebook's owner, Meta, is testing whether human phone workers, not artificial intelligence, handle the phone calls placed by its new AI assistant, Muse, according to internal company posts reviewed by Reuters. … Meta calls the setup a "human concierge," meaning a trained employee in a call center can pick up the request and place the call themselves. … Regular Muse users testing the public phone feature don't currently get that same choice [to opt out], and Meta hasn't said whether or when they will.
author: Suzanne Kantra
notes: Reuters/Techlicious Sep 22: human concierge behind Muse calls; public beta lacks employee opt-out.

quote: "The day after I said I wanted help saving money for a fancy vacation," he wrote, "Muse offered to 'wire your savings tracker to your real balance' if I just tapped a few buttons and linked the data from my checking and savings accounts." … Muse suggested letting it scan his entire email inbox, take pictures of important documents, photograph his meals to track their calories, and share when his passport and license expired. "Every suggested interaction with Muse started to feel like a guise for me to upload more data about myself for Meta to see," Rogers opined.
author: Frank Landymore
notes: Futurism Sep 22 synthesizing Aten + Wired Rogers data-upsell creepiness.
